..(Saturday night through Thursday)
Issued at 500 AM EDT FRI OCT 9 2026

The extended portion of the forecast looks to be on track with 
the idea of the remains of Isaias exiting to the east Sunday and
early Monday followed by drying in its wake as ridging aloft
builds into the state from the southwest. A nearby front,
initially to the north of Kentucky, could become a factor in our 
weather by the middle of next week. 

The previous long term discussion follows:

At the start of the extended period, all eyes will shift
towards the remnants of Hurricane Isaias. Model and ensemble
guidance continue to meander west and east with the storm track as
Isaias approaches the Gulf coastline. Previous guidance has
generally continued shifting the expected path west; however,
some of the latest 12Z guidance has trended back east a bit. As
Hurricane Isaias makes landfall and starts its trek north towards
the Tennessee Valley, it will be greeted by the subtropical jet
and enter a highly sheared environment. This will help weaken the
storm as it gets closer to eastern Kentucky. This will occur as
an amplified upper-level ridge across the Eastern US, with 500 mb
heights over the Commonwealth near 584-588 dam early on Saturday,
slowly departs northeast.

Showers and a few thunderstorms will spread initially across the 
area from south to north on Saturday (then southeast to northwest
at times) under downsloping easterly or southeasterly winds. 
Winds should gradually increase through the afternoon, peaking 
between midnight and 8 AM Sunday. These easterly gusts could 
generally range from 20-30 mph away from the high terrain 
bordering Tennessee and Virginia. For those high terrain areas 
near the state border with Tennessee and Virginia, wind gusts of 
35-45 mph are becoming more probable, with the NBM, LREF, and REFS
ensembles all showing at least a 55% chance of exposed mountain 
tops near Cumberland, such as Black Mountain, seeing wind gusts 
around or north of 40 mph. The peak gust timing in these areas 
ranges from 8 PM Saturday through 8 AM Sunday. Looking at model 
soundings near Bell, Harlan, and Letcher counties, winds aloft 
were as strong as 50-55 mph just below the the top of the
inversion, with stable lower levels and conditionally unstable 
layers with weaker winds further above the inversion. Mountain 
waves could be a possibility, which will be something that bears 
watching as higher-resolution model runs become more readily 
available.

With downslope flow expected, lower sfc dew points than NBM
deterministic are probable. To account for this on both Saturday 
and Sunday, forecasted dew points were lowered below the 
deterministic NBM using raw model guidance. Low temperatures will 
generally remain in the upper 50s to low 60s both Saturday and 
Sunday nights. Previously, high temperatures Saturday were wide- 
ranging as the ensembles had upper 60s to mid-80s as possibilities.
This was largely due to variability in timing for the storms 
arrival to the area. A sooner arrival meant more clouds and lower 
temperatures, whereas a delayed arrival led to more sunshine and 
ample heating into the mid-80s. However, the latest guidance has 
started to come into better agreement, narrowing the spread into 
the upper 60s to low 70s. Keep in mind the above scenarios can 
still drive high temperatures up or down based on when the 
remnants of Isaias work in here. Latest data has trended toward a 
quicker arrival and thus a cloudier start to Saturday. For this 
reason, high temperatures were lowered from the upper 70s in 
yesterdays forecast to the low-to-mid 70s for this package. The 
low 70s are around the 75th percentile of model and ensemble 
guidance.

As low-level flow turns southerly around the departing high, deep
moisture associated with Isaias will begin creeping northward.
PWATs will climb toward 1.0-1.3 inches near the Tennessee border
by Saturday morning, bringing shower and thunderstorm chances to
the area from the south. The timing of rain arrival will be
earliest along the state line with Tennessee and Virginia,
potentially starting as early as 6-8 AM Saturday. Shower and
thunderstorm chances will increase through the day Saturday,
overnight, and into Sunday. By the time the system reaches the 
Tennessee Valley to Lower OH Valley on Sunday, it becomes post-
tropical and follows the upper-level westerly and southwesterly 
flow east into the Mid-Atlantic region by Monday. Rain is likely 
across eastern Kentucky through much of Sunday, accompanied by 
isolated to scattered thunderstorm chances.

Broad southwesterly flow aloft between the Atlantic ridge and
western troughing will help channel the tropical moisture plume
from the Gulf low into the Ohio Valley. This will surge PWAT
values across the JKL CWA Sunday morning into early Sunday
afternoon, with forecasted PWATs falling within the 90th
